tagline.text: La Union's secret waterfall, spilling down through a rock canyon

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,000 per person (day trip from San Juan)

children.text: A two-tier waterfall about 15m tall on the upper Baroro River, inland in San Gabriel, La Union. Smooth rock canyon walls, a deep green pool, and a bamboo raft ride combine to make it a great half-day addition to a San Juan beach trip.
Tangadan Falls hides in a mountain valley in the village of Amontoc, San Gabriel, La Union province, bordering the town of Bagulin. It sits about
20km

into the mountains east of the surf town of San Juan, where the upper Baroro River drops over layered rock at the end of a carved-out canyon. It's the signature spot to experience "mountains and rivers" in La Union, a province better known for beaches and surfing, and on weekends travelers staying in San Juan often charter a tricycle or van for a half-day visit.
The falls have a two-tier structure: a main drop about

(50 feet) tall, plus smaller streams running beside and above it. Below the falls, a deep, dark-green pool spreads out wide, ringed by sandstone cliffs with clearly layered bedding, giving the feeling of stepping into a small canyon. In the morning sun, the water glows emerald, while in the afternoon the cliffs cast cool shade.

A locally run bamboo raft can take you right up to the base of the falls to feel the spray, and renting a life vest to swim in the pool or jump from the lower rocks is popular too. The falls used to be known for cliff diving from higher rocks, but the highest points are now off-limits due to the risk of accidents, so follow your guide's instructions.

Access is managed through registration at the San Gabriel municipal office, with a local guide required, and the route in passes rice paddies and mountain village scenery for a taste of rural life along the way. It suits travelers who enjoy light trekking and swimming, and anyone in San Juan looking for something to do on a day with no waves.
Local residents pull a bamboo raft by rope right up to the base of the falls. Feeling the spray up close is the highlight of a Tangadan visit.
The pool below the falls is deep and wide, good for floating around in a life vest. The water is cold, so ease in gradually before you swim.
You can jump into the pool from the lower rocks your guide permits. Only jump after checking the water depth and rock position with your guide.
Climb the rocks beside the main falls to see the smaller stream and pool above. The canyon view looking down from up top photographs well.

The sandstone cliffs, with their clearly layered bedding, contrast beautifully with the green water, making for a good shot from almost any angle. Early morning, when there are fewer people, is the best time to shoot.

blocks.title: Trek along the paddies and river

children.text: Besides the newly built stairway, there's also an old route crossing rice paddies and the Baroro River. If you have time to spare, ask your guide about the old route for a taste of the countryside.

blocks.title: A half-day paired with San Juan

children.text: The most popular plan is to visit the falls in the morning and catch the sunset at San Juan beach in the afternoon. It also pairs well with the Ma-Cho Temple in San Fernando on the same day.
Set out from your San Juan accommodation by chartered tricycle or van
Register at the San Gabriel municipal office, pay the entrance fee, get assigned a guide
Continue to the Amontoc trailhead by habal-habal (motorbike) or vehicle
Trek in via the stairway or the paddy trail to reach the falls
Bamboo raft, swimming, viewing the upper falls, and photos
Return to the trailhead, change clothes, head to San Gabriel town
Lunch in San Fernando, stop by the Ma-Cho Temple, then back to San Juan

Registration at the municipal office is usually available from early morning, though hours can change on holidays and event days. On weekends, group tours start arriving after 10 AM, so set out as early as you can. Timing your visit for a day when San Juan's waves are too small or too rough is a good way to fill out your trip without giving up surfing time. Coming from Baguio, the easiest route is down Naguilian Road to San Fernando and then into San Gabriel — allow about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
one way. About
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
at the falls is enough for the raft, swimming, and photos combined.
Take a northbound bus from Partas, Viron, or a similar line from the Cubao or Pasay terminal in Manila and get off in San Fernando or San Juan, La Union. It takes about
5–7 hours
, with a one-way fare of around
. Seeing only the falls and returning the same day isn't realistic, so plan to base yourself in San Juan for at least one night.
Chartering a tricycle from San Juan or San Fernando to San Gabriel town takes about
40–50 minutes
, for a round trip fare of around
per tricycle. Agree in advance on whether the fare includes waiting time.
Jeepneys to San Gabriel also run from San Fernando town, but service is infrequent, and you'll still need a habal-habal (round trip about
per person) from the municipal office to the falls entrance.
Follow the road from San Juan toward San Gabriel for about
40 minutes–1 hour

to reach the municipal office. The final stretch to the trailhead is a narrow, steep mountain road, so an SUV or local vehicle is safer than a small car — if you're not comfortable driving it, hire a van with a driver.
From the trailhead to the falls takes about
15–30 minutes
via the concrete stairway, or about
1 hour
via the old route across the paddies and river. The climb back up the stairs is tougher than it looks, so bring plenty of water.
The
November–May
dry season, when the trail is dry and the water clear, is the safest and most pleasant time to go. In
December–February
the stream runs quite cold, so midday is the best time to swim, while
March–May
, with midday temperatures climbing to
, is when a cool dip in the stream feels best. That said, toward the end of the dry season, lower water levels can thin out the falls.
During the
June–October

rainy season, higher water volume makes the falls more dramatic, but the water can turn muddy and the river level can rise suddenly. The municipal office sometimes closes access right after heavy rain or during typhoon warnings, so if you're visiting in the rainy season, aim for 2–3 days after the rain stops, once the water has cleared, and check whether it's open before you set out.

There's almost no traveler accommodation around the falls or in San Gabriel itself, so most visitors stay in the beach town of San Juan or the provincial capital, San Fernando, and visit as a day trip. Hostel dorms along San Juan's beach road run about
a night, guesthouses and resorts run about
, and business hotels in San Fernando town are available from about

Near the falls entrance there's little more than a small sari-sari store and a few simple food stalls, so it's best to bring your own drinks and snacks. On the way back, stop in San Fernando to cool off with bagnet, Ilocano-style crispy fried pork belly, pinakbet, a vegetable stew, or halo-halo topped with ube and leche flan. Back in San Juan, plenty of surfer-run cafés and brunch spots make for a good late lunch after your swim.
You can't enter without a guide. Be sure to register first at the San Gabriel municipal office and get assigned a guide.
Operating hours generally run
6 AM to 5 PM
. Arrive at the trailhead by 2 PM at the latest to explore at an unhurried pace.
Wear non-slip sandals or aqua shoes. The stairs and riverside rocks are very slippery with moss.
Put your phone and camera in a waterproof pouch, and leave electronics behind when you ride the raft, since you'll take the spray head-on.
There are simple changing areas near the trailhead, but facilities are basic. Bring a change of clothes, a towel, and a plastic bag.
Phone signal is weak once you're in the mountains. Agree on a pickup time with your driver in advance.
Only cash is accepted, so bring small bills for the entrance fee, guide fee, and habal-habal fare.
Carry out all your trash, and don't use shampoo or soap in the pool.

The pool below the falls is deep, and the water swirls right beneath the falls, which can be dangerous even for confident swimmers. Wear a life vest even if you swim well, and never jump from the rocks that have been closed off.
Rain upstream can raise the water level and cloud the water within a short time. If the water turns murky, get out right away.
Access may be restricted after a typhoon or heavy rain, so check the latest notice through the municipal office or your accommodation.
The habal-habal ride runs along a steep, unpaved road. Ask for a helmet, and tell the driver to slow down if you feel unsafe.
Children and elderly travelers may find the uphill stairs and slippery rocks physically demanding.
Swimming or jumping after drinking is very dangerous — avoid it entirely.
